module.title: Unit 6: Free Time: Hobbies, Like + -ing & Can / Can't
module.objective: Talk about hobbies and interests, use the 'like + -ing' pattern, express possession with 'have/has got', and describe abilities with 'can/can't'.

content.summary: Welcome to your Reading Mission! In this unit, you will read a fun passage about teenagers and their free-time hobbies. You will learn how people talk about what they like doing, what gadgets they have got, and what they can or can't do. By the end of this mission, you will feel confident reading short texts about hobbies and abilities. Let's get started!

linguisticTarget.grammar: Like + verb-ing to express preferences (e.g., I like swimming), have/has got for possession (e.g., She's got a guitar), and can/can't for ability (e.g., He can play the piano, but he can't sing).
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Hobbies and free-time activities (swimming, reading, cooking, drawing, playing football), gadgets (tablet, smartphone, laptop, games console), and musical instruments.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming the passage first to understand the main topic, then scanning for specific details such as names, hobbies, and abilities. Look for key patterns like 'like + -ing', 'have/has got', and 'can/can't' to help you understand the text quickly.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 passage about teenagers' hobbies and free time.
Identify key details including who likes which hobby, what gadgets they have got, and what they can or can't do.
Recognize and understand the grammar patterns 'like + -ing', 'have/has got', and 'can/can't' in context.
Build vocabulary related to hobbies, gadgets, and abilities by seeing words used naturally in a passage.

contextWarmup.prompt: Read this sentence: 'Anna likes painting and she can draw very well.' What does Anna enjoy doing in her free time?
contextWarmup.explanation: The sentence says Anna 'likes painting' and 'can draw very well.' The key words 'likes painting' and 'can draw' tell us her hobby is art — painting and drawing. Well done if you spotted the 'like + -ing' pattern!

rules: Like + -ing: When you want to say what hobby you enjoy, use 'like' followed by a verb with '-ing'. For example: 'I like reading books.' For he/she/it, add -s to 'like': 'She likes cooking.'

Have/Has got: Use 'have got' (I/you/we/they) or 'has got' (he/she/it) to say what you own or possess. For example: 'I've got a laptop.' 'He's got a guitar.' In negative: 'I haven't got a tablet.' 'She hasn't got headphones.'

Can/Can't for ability: Use 'can' + base verb (no -ing, no -s) to say what someone is able to do. For example: 'I can swim.' 'She can play the piano.' Use 'can't' for things you are not able to do: 'He can't cook.'
When reading, look for signal words: 'like/likes' followed by '-ing' tells you about preferences. 'Have got / has got' tells you about possessions. 'Can / can't' tells you about abilities.
Remember: after 'can' or 'can't', always use the base form of the verb — never add '-ing' or '-s'. For example: 'She can swim' (NOT 'She can swimming' or 'She can swims').

commonTrap.trapTitle: Common Beginner Pitfall: Mixing Up 'like + -ing' and 'can + base verb'
commonTrap.explanation: Many beginners confuse the verb forms after 'like' and 'can'. After 'like', you must add '-ing' to the verb. After 'can', you must use the base form (no -ing). Mixing these up is a very common mistake at A1 level!
commonTrap.wrong: I like swim. / She can swimming.
commonTrap.correct: I like swimming. / She can swim.

grammarFormulas.title: Sentence Structure with Like + -ing, Have/Has Got & Can/Can't
grammarFormulas.description: Assemble and swap sentence blocks to explore affirmative, negative, and question patterns:

items.collocation: I like swimming in the pool after school.
She likes drawing pictures of animals.
My mum likes cooking Italian food.
He's got a new guitar and he can play it really well.
We like playing football at the weekend.
He's got the ability to play two instruments.
What do you do in your free time?
Can you play a musical instrument?

content.context: Three teenagers — Tom, Mia, and Leo — are writing about their hobbies and free-time activities for a school magazine. Read about what they like doing, what gadgets they have got, and what they can and can't do.
content.text:
Hi! My name is Tom. I'm thirteen. In my free time, I like playing football with my friends. I've got a new smartphone and I like taking photos. I can run very fast, but I can't swim.

Hello! I'm Mia. I'm twelve. I like drawing and painting. I've got a tablet and I use it for my art. I can play the guitar, but I can't cook! My mum likes cooking, so that's OK.

Hey! I'm Leo. I'm fourteen. I like playing computer games on my games console. I've also got an e-reader because I like reading adventure books. I can speak two languages — English and Spanish — but I can't play any musical instruments. Have you got a hobby?

highlights.note: 'Like + -ing' pattern: this shows Tom enjoys football as a hobby.
Contraction of 'I have got' — used to talk about possessions.
'Can + base verb' shows ability. Tom is able to run fast.
'Can't + base verb' shows inability. Tom is not able to swim.
'Likes + -ing' with third person (Mum). Notice the -s on 'likes'.
A hobby word: the activity of making pictures with a pencil or pen.
A device used to play video games, such as PlayStation or Xbox.
An electronic device for reading digital books and magazines.

gistQuestion.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Three teenagers talking about their hobbies, gadgets, and abilities.
Three teenagers talking about their school subjects.
Three teenagers talking about their families and pets.
gistQuestion.explanation: The passage is about Tom, Mia, and Leo sharing what they like doing in their free time, what gadgets they have got, and what they can and can't do. The main topic is hobbies and abilities.

detailQuestions.prompt: What does Tom like doing in his free time?
options: He likes playing football and taking photos.
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'I like playing football with my friends' and 'I like taking photos.' Both hobbies belong to Tom.

detailQuestions.prompt: What can Mia do, and what can't she do?
options: She can play the guitar, but she can't cook.
She can cook, but she can't play the guitar.
She can swim, but she can't draw.
detailQuestions.explanation: Mia says: 'I can play the guitar, but I can't cook!' This clearly tells us her ability and inability.

detailQuestions.prompt: Why has Leo got an e-reader?
options: Because he likes reading adventure books.
Because he likes playing computer games.
detailQuestions.explanation: Leo says: 'I've also got an e-reader because I like reading adventure books.' The word 'because' connects his possession (e-reader) with his hobby (reading).

detailQuestions.prompt: How many languages can Leo speak?
detailQuestions.explanation: Leo says: 'I can speak two languages — English and Spanish.' The number 'two' and the dash give us the specific detail.

questions.question: According to the passage, which person can't swim?
questions.explanation: Tom says: 'I can run very fast, but I can't swim.' The word 'can't' clearly tells us Tom is unable to swim.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the correct 'like + -ing' pattern?
questions.explanation: With 'she' (third person singular), we use 'likes' (with -s), and the verb after 'like' must have '-ing'. So 'She likes drawing pictures' is correct.

questions.question: What gadget has Mia got?
questions.explanation: Mia says: 'I've got a tablet and I use it for my art.' The passage clearly states she has a tablet.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence about ability:
questions.explanation: After 'can', we always use the base form of the verb — no '-ing' and no '-s'. So 'He can speak' is the correct form.

questions.question: Who likes cooking in the passage?
questions.explanation: Mia says: 'I can't cook! My mum likes cooking, so that's OK.' It is Mia's mum who likes cooking, not Mia herself.

questions.question: What does 'I've got a new smartphone' mean?
questions.explanation: 'I've got' is a contraction of 'I have got', which means 'I have' or 'I possess'. It tells us about something you own right now.

questions.question: What can't Leo do?
options: He can't play any musical instruments.
questions.answer: He can't play any musical instruments.
questions.explanation: Leo says: 'I can't play any musical instruments.' He clearly states this inability. He can read (he's got an e-reader) and he can speak English and Spanish.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Talking About Hobbies and What We Can Do

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear Olivia tell Chloe about her brother Patrick's new friend, Freddie. They talk about what Freddie looks like, what hobbies he likes doing, and what he can and can't do. Listen carefully for the pattern 'like + -ing' (for example, 'He likes playing football') and 'can / can't' (for example, 'He can swim' or 'He can't cook'). Also listen for 'has got / have got' when they describe what someone has. Focus on the key words about hobbies and free-time activities. A useful strategy is to listen for the verb after 'like' — it will always end in '-ing'. When you hear 'can' or 'can't', pay attention to whether the speaker sounds positive or negative — 'can't' has a stronger, shorter vowel sound in British English.
learningObjectives: Identify hobbies and free-time activities mentioned in a conversation.
Recognise the pattern 'like + -ing' when speakers talk about things they enjoy.
Understand 'can' and 'can't' when speakers talk about abilities.
Recognise 'has got / have got' when speakers describe what someone has.

keyPhrases.note: Use 'like + -ing' to talk about hobbies. The verb after 'like' always takes the -ing form.
Use 'can + base verb' (no 'to') to talk about ability. 'Can' is the same for all subjects.

keyPhrases.meaning: Dia tidak bisa memasak dengan baik.
keyPhrases.note: Use 'can't' (cannot) to say someone does not have the ability to do something.
Use 'has got' (he's got) to talk about possession. 'He's got' is the contracted spoken form of 'he has got'.

keyPhrases.phrase: What does he like doing in his free time?
keyPhrases.meaning: Apa yang dia suka lakukan di waktu luangnya?
keyPhrases.note: A common question to ask about someone's hobbies. Listen for 'like doing' as a question pattern.

keyPhrases.phrase: I like reading and listening to music.
keyPhrases.meaning: Saya suka membaca dan mendengarkan musik.
keyPhrases.note: You can list multiple hobbies using 'and' between them. Each hobby uses the -ing form after 'like'.

connectedSpeech.note: In natural speech, the final 'g' in '-ing' words often drops, so 'playing' sounds like 'playin'. This is very common in casual British English.
'Has got' contracts to 'he's got' in fast speech. The 'ha-' disappears and only the /z/ sound remains attached to 'he'.
In British English, 'can't' is pronounced /kɑːnt/ with a long 'ah' vowel. This is different from 'can' /kæn/ which has a short vowel. Listen for this vowel difference to tell them apart.
'What does' blends together in fast speech. The 't' in 'what' links to 'does', and 'does' reduces to /dəz/. 'He' often loses its /h/ and becomes just /i/.

connectedSpeech.slow: He is really good at it.
connectedSpeech.note: 'He is' contracts to 'he's'. The word 'at' reduces to /ət/ in fast speech because it is an unstressed function word.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: My Free Time and Hobbies

content.summary: In this lesson, you will learn how to write sentences and short paragraphs about your hobbies and free time. You will practise using 'like + -ing' to talk about things you enjoy, 'have/has got' to talk about things you own, and 'can/can't' to talk about your abilities. Follow the blueprint steps below to build clear, correct sentences about your free time.

blueprintItems.title: Say What You Like Doing
blueprintItems.example: I like playing football after school.

blueprintItems.title: Say What You Have Got
blueprintItems.example: She has got a new guitar.

blueprintItems.title: Say What You Can or Can't Do
blueprintItems.example: I can swim, but I can't play tennis.

blueprintItems.title: Combine Ideas in a Short Paragraph
blueprintItems.example: I like drawing pictures. I have got many coloured pencils. I can draw animals, but I can't draw people very well.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always start a sentence with a capital letter and end it with a full stop.
mechanicsRules.why: Every sentence in English must begin with a capital letter and finish with a full stop, question mark, or exclamation mark.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'likes' (with an 's') for he, she, and it. Use 'like' (no 's') for I, you, we, and they.
mechanicsRules.why: In the present simple tense, third-person singular subjects (he, she, it) need an 's' on the verb.

mechanicsRules.rule: After 'like', always use the verb with '-ing'. Do not use the base form.
mechanicsRules.why: The pattern is 'like + verb-ing'. The '-ing' form must follow 'like' to express enjoyment.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'has got' for he, she, and it. Use 'have got' for I, you, we, and they.
mechanicsRules.why: Third-person singular subjects use 'has got', while all other subjects use 'have got'.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Talking About Hobbies, Free Time & What You Can Do

content.summary: In this speaking lab, you will practise talking about your hobbies, free time activities, and abilities. You will use 'like + -ing' to say what you enjoy, 'have got / has got' to talk about things you own, and 'can / can't' to describe what you are able or unable to do. Good pronunciation of '-ing' endings, clear stress on key words, and correct rising and falling intonation in questions and statements will help you sound natural and confident.
content.audioGuidance: Pay special attention to the '-ing' ending in words like 'playing', 'reading', and 'listening'. The 'ng' sound /ŋ/ is made at the back of your mouth — do not say 'in' instead of 'ing'. For 'can', use the weak form /kən/ in positive sentences ('I can swim') and the strong form /kænt/ for 'can't'. Use rising intonation for yes/no questions ('Can you swim?') and falling intonation for statements ('I like reading books.').

pillars.name: The '-ing' Ending
pillars.explanation: When you say 'playing', 'reading', or 'listening', make sure the final sound is /ɪŋ/, not /ɪn/. The 'ng' sound comes from the back of your tongue touching the soft part of the roof of your mouth. Practise: 'sing', 'ring', 'playing'.

pillars.name: Weak 'can' vs Strong 'can't'
pillars.explanation: In natural speech, 'can' is usually weak: /kən/. For example, 'I can swim' sounds like 'I k'n swim'. But 'can't' is always strong and clear: /kɑːnt/ (British) or /kænt/ (American). The difference in stress helps your listener understand you.

pillars.name: Intonation in Questions and Statements
pillars.target: Natural rising and falling pitch patterns
pillars.explanation: Yes/no questions like 'Do you like swimming?' and 'Can you play guitar?' use rising intonation — your voice goes up at the end. Statements like 'I like reading books' and 'I can't cook' use falling intonation — your voice goes down at the end. This makes your English sound clear and natural.

pillars.name: Sentence Stress on Content Words
pillars.explanation: In English, we stress the important words: nouns, verbs, adjectives. For example: 'I LIKE PLAYING FOOTball.' The words 'like', 'playing', and 'football' are louder and longer. Small words like 'I', 'to', and 'a' are quick and soft.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The stress stays on the first syllable 'HOB' in both 'hobby' and 'hobbies'. The ending changes but the rhythm stays the same.
When we add '-ing' to 'play', the stress remains on 'PLAY'. The '-ing' is short and unstressed. This pattern is the same for 'reading', 'singing', 'cooking'.
The stress stays on 'LIS' when we add '-ing'. Notice that 'listening' has three syllables, but only the first one is strong. Also, the 't' in 'listen' is silent.
The stress stays on 'TAR' in both 'guitar' and 'guitarist'. The first syllable 'gui' is always quick and soft.

drills.hint: Stress 'LIKE', 'PLAY', and 'FOOT'. Make sure 'playing' ends with /ŋ/, not /n/.
Say 'likes' with a clear /s/ at the end. 'Listening' has three syllables: LIS-ten-ing. The 't' is silent.
Use the weak form /kən/ for 'can'. Your voice should rise at the end because this is a yes/no question.

drills.targetText: I can't cook, but I can make a sandwich.
drills.phonetic: /aɪ kɑːnt kʊk | bʌt aɪ kən meɪk ə ˈsæn.wɪdʒ/
drills.hint: Say 'CAN'T' loudly and clearly. Then say 'can' quickly and softly before 'make'. This contrast helps your listener understand.

drills.targetText: I have got a smartphone and a tablet.
drills.phonetic: /aɪ hæv ɡɒt ə ˈsmɑːt.fəʊn ənd ə ˈtæb.lɪt/
drills.focus: 'Have got' structure and compound noun stress
drills.hint: Stress 'SMART' in 'smartphone' and 'TAB' in 'tablet'. These are the important content words.

drills.targetText: What do you like doing in your free time?
drills.phonetic: /wɒt duː juː laɪk ˈduː.ɪŋ ɪn jɔː friː taɪm/
drills.hint: This is a Wh-question, so your voice should fall at the end on 'free TIME'. Stress 'LIKE', 'DO-ing', 'FREE', and 'TIME'.

roleplay.context: You are at school talking to your teacher, Mr. Khoirul, about your free time, your hobbies, and the gadgets you use every day. Mr. Khoirul asks you questions and you answer using 'like + -ing', 'have got', and 'can / can't'. Speak clearly and try to use full sentences.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about your hobbies and free time. Use 'like + -ing' and 'can / can't'. Follow the three story points below. Speak for about 30 seconds.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now it is your turn to speak! Tell me about your hobbies and what you do in your free time. What do you like doing? What can you do? What can't you do? Follow the three points and speak clearly.
storyPoints: Say what hobbies you have and what you like doing in your free time.
Talk about one thing you can do well and one thing you can't do.
Say what gadget you have got and how you use it for your hobby.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I like playing football and reading books. I can swim but I can't play guitar. I have got a tablet and I use it to watch videos.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ laɪk ˈpleɪ.ɪŋ ˈfʊt.bɔːl ənd ˈriː.dɪŋ bʊks | aɪ kən swɪm bʌt aɪ kɑːnt pleɪ ɡɪˈtɑːr | aɪ hæv ɡɒt ə ˈtæb.lɪt ənd aɪ juːz ɪt tə wɒtʃ ˈvɪd.i.əʊz/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember to use 'like + -ing' for hobbies. Use 'can' for things you are able to do and 'can't' for things you are not able to do. Use 'have got' to talk about your gadgets.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task checks if you can combine three key structures from this unit: 'like + -ing' for preferences, 'can / can't' for abilities, and 'have got' for possessions. Speaking in connected sentences helps build fluency.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about your best friend's hobbies and abilities. Use 'likes + -ing', 'has got', and 'can / can't'. Follow the three story points below.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now tell me about your best friend. What does your friend like doing? What has your friend got? What can or can't your friend do? Follow the three points.
storyPoints: Say your friend's name and what he or she likes doing.
Talk about what gadgets your friend has got.
Say one thing your friend can do and one thing he or she can't do.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: My best friend is Rina. She likes singing and drawing. She has got a smartphone. She can dance but she can't cook.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /maɪ best frend ɪz ˈriː.nə | ʃiː laɪks ˈsɪŋ.ɪŋ ənd ˈdrɔː.ɪŋ | ʃiː hæz ɡɒt ə ˈsmɑːt.fəʊn | ʃiː kən dɑːns bʌt ʃiː kɑːnt kʊk/
practicumQuestions.hint: For your friend, use 'likes' with an 's' and 'has got' instead of 'have got'. Remember the third person form!
practicumQuestions.explanation: This task practises third person forms: 'likes + -ing' and 'has got'. Telling a story about someone else helps you remember to add '-s' to verbs and use 'has' instead of 'have'.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are at a new school. It is your first day. Your new classmate wants to know about your hobbies and what you can do. You answer questions about your free time activities, your abilities, and the gadgets you own.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are the new student. Your classmate (played by the AI tutor) asks you questions. Answer using 'like + -ing', 'can / can't', and 'have got'. Be friendly and give full answers.
practicumQuestions.instruction: Your new classmate asks about your hobbies. Answer the questions using 'like + -ing' and 'can / can't'. Give full sentences.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hi! Welcome to our school! I want to know about you. What do you like doing after school?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I like playing video games and watching movies after school.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ laɪk ˈpleɪ.ɪŋ ˈvɪd.i.əʊ ɡeɪmz ənd ˈwɒtʃ.ɪŋ ˈmuː.viz ˈɑːf.tər skuːl/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'I like' followed by a verb with '-ing'. For example: 'I like playing...' or 'I like watching...'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: In this roleplay, you practise answering questions about hobbies naturally. Using 'like + -ing' in a real conversation helps you become more fluent.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are at a sports club. The coach wants to know what sports and activities you can and can't do before putting you in a group. You need to tell the coach about your abilities.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a young person joining a sports club. The coach (played by the AI tutor) asks about your abilities. Answer honestly using 'can' and 'can't'.
practicumQuestions.instruction: The sports coach asks what you can do. Tell the coach about your abilities using 'can' and 'can't'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Welcome to the sports club! Tell me, can you swim?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yes, I can swim. But I can't play tennis.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /jes aɪ kən swɪm | bʌt aɪ kɑːnt pleɪ ˈten.ɪs/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'Yes, I can' or 'No, I can't' to answer. Then add more information. Remember: 'can' is weak /kən/ but 'can't' is strong /kɑːnt/.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay focuses on using 'can' and 'can't' to talk about physical abilities. Practising in a sports club scenario makes the language feel real and useful.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are at an electronics shop with your parent. The shop assistant asks what gadgets you have got and what you use them for. You explain what you own and how you use your gadgets for your hobbies.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a young customer in an electronics shop. The shop assistant (played by the AI tutor) asks about your gadgets. Answer using 'have got' and explain how you use them.
practicumQuestions.instruction: The shop assistant asks about your gadgets. Tell them what you have got and what you use them for.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Good afternoon! What gadgets have you got at home?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I have got a tablet and a smartphone. I use my tablet for watching videos and I use my smartphone for listening to music.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ hæv ɡɒt ə ˈtæb.lɪt ənd ə ˈsmɑːt.fəʊn | aɪ juːz maɪ ˈtæb.lɪt fɔːr ˈwɒtʃ.ɪŋ ˈvɪd.i.əʊz ənd aɪ juːz maɪ ˈsmɑːt.fəʊn fɔːr ˈlɪs.ən.ɪŋ tə ˈmjuː.zɪk/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'I have got...' to say what you own. Then say 'I use it for + -ing' to explain what you do with it.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay combines 'have got' for possession with 'for + -ing' to describe purpose. It connects gadgets to hobbies, which is a natural and useful conversation topic.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are talking to your teacher, Mr. Khoirul, about a weekend plan. He wants to know what activities you like doing on weekends and what new things you want to try. You discuss your free time preferences and abilities.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student talking to Mr. Khoirul (played by the AI tutor) about your weekend. Answer his questions about what you like doing, what you can do, and what you want to try.
practicumQuestions.instruction: Mr. Khoirul asks about your weekend plans. Talk about what you like doing and what you can or can't do.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! The weekend is coming. What do you like doing on Saturdays?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: On Saturdays, I like riding my bike and playing with my friends. I can ride a bike but I can't skateboard.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɒn ˈsæt.ə.deɪz aɪ laɪk ˈraɪ.dɪŋ maɪ baɪk ənd ˈpleɪ.ɪŋ wɪð maɪ frendz | aɪ kən raɪd ə baɪk bʌt aɪ kɑːnt ˈskeɪt.bɔːd/
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'On Saturdays, I like...' and add '-ing' verbs. Then use 'can' and 'can't' to talk about your abilities.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay brings together all three structures from the unit in a natural weekend conversation. Combining 'like + -ing' with 'can / can't' shows you can use multiple structures together.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say each hobby and free time word clearly. Focus on correct pronunciation of the '-ing' ending and the hobby vocabulary from this unit.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this word clearly. Focus on the correct sounds.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: swimming, cooking, drawing, reading, skateboarding
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈswɪm.ɪŋ/, /ˈkʊk.ɪŋ/, /ˈdrɔː.ɪŋ/, /ˈriː.dɪŋ/, /ˈskeɪt.bɔː.dɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Each word ends with '-ing' /ɪŋ/. Make sure you say the /ŋ/ sound at the back of your mouth, not /n/. 'Skateboarding' has three syllables: SKATE-boar-ding.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Hobby vocabulary with '-ing' forms is essential for this unit. Correct pronunciation of /ɪŋ/ is a common challenge. Practising these words individually builds confidence before using them in sentences.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentences aloud. Focus on using the correct grammar: 'like + -ing', 'have got', and 'can / can't'. Make sure you do not say 'like to play' — say 'like playing'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence. Be careful with the grammar structure.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: She likes cooking and she has got a new cookbook. She can make pasta but she can't make sushi.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ʃiː laɪks ˈkʊk.ɪŋ ənd ʃiː hæz ɡɒt ə njuː ˈkʊk.bʊk | ʃiː kən meɪk ˈpæs.tə bʌt ʃiː kɑːnt meɪk ˈsuː.ʃi/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember: with 'she', use 'likes' (with -s) and 'has got' (not 'have got'). After 'can' and 'can't', use the base verb without 'to': 'can make', not 'can to make'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill checks three grammar points at once: third person 'likes + -ing', 'has got' for possession, and 'can / can't + base verb' for ability. Saying the full sentence helps you internalise the correct patterns.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say each pair of words. Notice how the stress stays on the same syllable or shifts. Tap or clap on the stressed syllable to feel the rhythm.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen to the stress pattern and repeat. Clap on the strong syllable.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: PLAY → PLAY-ing, FOOT-ball → FOOT-ball-er, gui-TAR → gui-TAR-ist, PHO-to → pho-TOG-ra-phy
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /pleɪ/ → /ˈpleɪ.ɪŋ/, /ˈfʊt.bɔːl/ → /ˈfʊt.bɔː.lər/, /ɡɪˈtɑːr/ → /ɡɪˈtɑː.rɪst/, /ˈfəʊ.təʊ/ → /fəˈtɒɡ.rə.fi/
practicumQuestions.hint: Notice: 'play' and 'playing' keep stress on 'PLAY'. 'Football' and 'footballer' keep stress on 'FOOT'. But 'photo' has stress on 'PHO', while 'photography' shifts stress to 'TOG'. This shift is important!
practicumQuestions.explanation: Syllable stress can stay the same or shift when a word gets longer. Most '-ing' forms keep the original stress. But some longer words like 'photography' shift the stress. Learning these patterns helps you sound more natural.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say each sentence with the correct intonation. Yes/no questions go UP at the end. Wh-questions and statements go DOWN at the end. Listen to the pattern and copy it.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say these sentences with the correct intonation. Remember: yes/no questions rise, statements and wh-questions fall.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Can you swim? ↗ | I can't swim. ↘ | What do you like doing? ↘ | Do you like reading? ↗ | I like playing football. ↘
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /kən juː swɪm ↗/ | /aɪ kɑːnt swɪm ↘/ | /wɒt duː juː laɪk ˈduː.ɪŋ ↘/ | /duː juː laɪk ˈriː.dɪŋ ↗/ | /aɪ laɪk ˈpleɪ.ɪŋ ˈfʊt.bɔːl ↘/
practicumQuestions.hint: For 'Can you swim?' and 'Do you like reading?', your voice goes UP at the end — these are yes/no questions. For 'What do you like doing?', 'I can't swim', and 'I like playing football', your voice goes DOWN — these are a wh-question and statements.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Intonation carries meaning in English. Rising intonation on yes/no questions signals that you expect a 'yes' or 'no' answer. Falling intonation on statements and wh-questions signals that you are giving information or asking for specific details. Mastering these patterns makes your speech much clearer.

reading.question: According to the passage, which person can't swim?
reading.explanation: Tom says: 'I can run very fast, but I can't swim.' The word 'can't' clearly tells us Tom is unable to swim.

reading.question: Which sentence uses the correct 'like + -ing' pattern?
reading.explanation: With 'she' (third person singular), we use 'likes' (with -s), and the verb after 'like' must have '-ing'. So 'She likes drawing pictures' is correct.

reading.question: What gadget has Mia got?
reading.explanation: Mia says: 'I've got a tablet and I use it for my art.' The passage clearly states she has a tablet.

reading.question: Choose the correct sentence about ability:
reading.explanation: After 'can', we always use the base form of the verb — no '-ing' and no '-s'. So 'He can speak' is the correct form.

reading.question: Who likes cooking in the passage?
reading.explanation: Mia says: 'I can't cook! My mum likes cooking, so that's OK.' It is Mia's mum who likes cooking, not Mia herself.

reading.question: What does 'I've got a new smartphone' mean?
reading.explanation: 'I've got' is a contraction of 'I have got', which means 'I have' or 'I possess'. It tells us about something you own right now.

reading.question: What can't Leo do?
options: He can't play any musical instruments.
reading.answer: He can't play any musical instruments.
reading.explanation: Leo says: 'I can't play any musical instruments.' He clearly states this inability. He can read (he's got an e-reader) and he can speak English and Spanish.

reading.question: What time does the train to London depart?
reading.explanation: Standard timetable questions provide specific morning departure times.

reading.question: Choose the correct past form: 'Yesterday, we _____ a new car.'
reading.explanation: 'Buy' is an irregular verb whose past simple form is 'bought'.

reading.question: What does Maria do every Saturday morning?
reading.explanation: A routine action in the simple present tense describing Saturday morning.

reading.question: Which question is grammatically correct?
reading.explanation: Standard question order: Question Word + Auxiliary (do) + Subject (you) + Verb (live).

reading.question: What is the opposite of 'expensive'?
reading.explanation: 'Cheap' means low in price, which is the direct opposite of 'expensive'.

reading.question: Choose the correct preposition: 'The keys are _____ the table.'
reading.explanation: We use 'on' when an object is physically resting on a surface.

reading.question: Which sentence expresses a future plan?
options: I am going to visit my grandmother tomorrow.
I visit my grandmother every day.
reading.answer: I am going to visit my grandmother tomorrow.
reading.explanation: 'Be going to' expresses a planned future intention.

reading.question: What can you buy at a pharmacy?
reading.explanation: Pharmacies specialize in dispensing medicines and healthcare supplies.

writing.prompt: Write 3 sentences about things you like doing in your free time. Use 'like + -ing' in each sentence.
writing.criteria: Each sentence must use the correct 'like + verb-ing' pattern. Sentences must start with a capital letter and end with a full stop. Use at least 3 different hobbies.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: I like playing video games after school. I like cooking dinner with my family. I like watching funny videos on my phone.

writing.prompt: Write 3 sentences about a family member. Use 'has got' or 'hasn't got' in each sentence to describe what they own or do not own.
writing.criteria: Each sentence must use 'has got' or 'hasn't got' correctly for a third-person singular subject (he/she). Sentences must be grammatically correct with proper capitalisation and punctuation.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: My brother has got a red bicycle. He has got two pet fish. He hasn't got a computer in his room.

writing.prompt: Write a short paragraph (at least 5 sentences) about yourself. Include what hobbies you like, what things you have got, and what you can or can't do. Use all three patterns: 'like + -ing', 'have/has got', and 'can/can't'.
writing.criteria: The paragraph must contain at least 5 sentences. It must correctly use 'like + -ing' at least once, 'have got' or 'haven't got' at least once, and 'can' or 'can't' at least once. All sentences must have correct capitalisation and punctuation. The writing should be clear and easy to understand.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: My name is Dani and I have got many hobbies. I like playing badminton with my friends at the weekend. I have got a good badminton racket. I can play well, but I can't win against my older brother. I also like drawing pictures. I haven't got many coloured pencils, but I can draw with a normal pencil.

writing.instruction: Susun kata-kata ini menjadi kalimat yang benar:

He is never late for school

Alex is taller than Leo

Our English lesson begins at 9 o'clock in the morning.
writing.explanation: Preposisi 'at' digunakan untuk penunjuk jam yang spesifik.

writing.instruction: Tuliskan kalimat sopan meminta segelas air menggunakan 'Can I':

writing.hint: Can I have a glass of water, please?
targetAnswers: Can I have a glass of water, please?
Can I have a glass of water please?

questions.instruction: Say each pair of words. Notice how the stress stays on the same syllable or shifts. Tap or clap on the stressed syllable to feel the rhythm.
questions.audioPrompt: Listen to the stress pattern and repeat. Clap on the strong syllable.
questions.targetSentence: PLAY → PLAY-ing, FOOT-ball → FOOT-ball-er, gui-TAR → gui-TAR-ist, PHO-to → pho-TOG-ra-phy
questions.hint: Notice: 'play' and 'playing' keep stress on 'PLAY'. 'Football' and 'footballer' keep stress on 'FOOT'. But 'photo' has stress on 'PHO', while 'photography' shifts stress to 'TOG'. This shift is important!
questions.explanation: Syllable stress can stay the same or shift when a word gets longer. Most '-ing' forms keep the original stress. But some longer words like 'photography' shift the stress. Learning these patterns helps you sound more natural.

questions.instruction: Say each sentence with the correct intonation. Yes/no questions go UP at the end. Wh-questions and statements go DOWN at the end. Listen to the pattern and copy it.
questions.audioPrompt: Say these sentences with the correct intonation. Remember: yes/no questions rise, statements and wh-questions fall.
questions.targetSentence: Can you swim? ↗ | I can't swim. ↘ | What do you like doing? ↘ | Do you like reading? ↗ | I like playing football. ↘
questions.phonetic: /kən juː swɪm ↗/ | /aɪ kɑːnt swɪm ↘/ | /wɒt duː juː laɪk ˈduː.ɪŋ ↘/ | /duː juː laɪk ˈriː.dɪŋ ↗/ | /aɪ laɪk ˈpleɪ.ɪŋ ˈfʊt.bɔːl ↘/
questions.hint: For 'Can you swim?' and 'Do you like reading?', your voice goes UP at the end — these are yes/no questions. For 'What do you like doing?', 'I can't swim', and 'I like playing football', your voice goes DOWN — these are a wh-question and statements.
questions.explanation: Intonation carries meaning in English. Rising intonation on yes/no questions signals that you expect a 'yes' or 'no' answer. Falling intonation on statements and wh-questions signals that you are giving information or asking for specific details. Mastering these patterns makes your speech much clearer.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are talking to your teacher, Mr. Khoirul, about a weekend plan. He wants to know what activities you like doing on weekends and what new things you want to try. You discuss your free time preferences and abilities.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student talking to Mr. Khoirul (played by the AI tutor) about your weekend. Answer his questions about what you like doing, what you can do, and what you want to try.
practicumQuestions.instruction: Mr. Khoirul asks about your weekend plans. Talk about what you like doing and what you can or can't do.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! The weekend is coming. What do you like doing on Saturdays?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: On Saturdays, I like riding my bike and playing with my friends. I can ride a bike but I can't skateboard.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɒn ˈsæt.ə.deɪz aɪ laɪk ˈraɪ.dɪŋ maɪ baɪk ənd ˈpleɪ.ɪŋ wɪð maɪ frendz | aɪ kən raɪd ə baɪk bʌt aɪ kɑːnt ˈskeɪt.bɔːd/
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'On Saturdays, I like...' and add '-ing' verbs. Then use 'can' and 'can't' to talk about your abilities.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay brings together all three structures from the unit in a natural weekend conversation. Combining 'like + -ing' with 'can / can't' shows you can use multiple structures together.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Hobby vocabulary with '-ing' forms is essential for this unit. Correct pronunciation of /ɪŋ/ is a common challenge. Practising these words individually builds confidence before using them in sentences.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentences aloud. Focus on using the correct grammar: 'like + -ing', 'have got', and 'can / can't'. Make sure you do not say 'like to play' — say 'like playing'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence. Be careful with the grammar structure.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: She likes cooking and she has got a new cookbook. She can make pasta but she can't make sushi.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ʃiː laɪks ˈkʊk.ɪŋ ənd ʃiː hæz ɡɒt ə njuː ˈkʊk.bʊk | ʃiː kən meɪk ˈpæs.tə bʌt ʃiː kɑːnt meɪk ˈsuː.ʃi/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember: with 'she', use 'likes' (with -s) and 'has got' (not 'have got'). After 'can' and 'can't', use the base verb without 'to': 'can make', not 'can to make'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill checks three grammar points at once: third person 'likes + -ing', 'has got' for possession, and 'can / can't + base verb' for ability. Saying the full sentence helps you internalise the correct patterns.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say each pair of words. Notice how the stress stays on the same syllable or shifts. Tap or clap on the stressed syllable to feel the rhythm.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen to the stress pattern and repeat. Clap on the strong syllable.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: PLAY → PLAY-ing, FOOT-ball → FOOT-ball-er, gui-TAR → gui-TAR-ist, PHO-to → pho-TOG-ra-phy
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /pleɪ/ → /ˈpleɪ.ɪŋ/, /ˈfʊt.bɔːl/ → /ˈfʊt.bɔː.lər/, /ɡɪˈtɑːr/ → /ɡɪˈtɑː.rɪst/, /ˈfəʊ.təʊ/ → /fəˈtɒɡ.rə.fi/
practicumQuestions.hint: Notice: 'play' and 'playing' keep stress on 'PLAY'. 'Football' and 'footballer' keep stress on 'FOOT'. But 'photo' has stress on 'PHO', while 'photography' shifts stress to 'TOG'. This shift is important!
practicumQuestions.explanation: Syllable stress can stay the same or shift when a word gets longer. Most '-ing' forms keep the original stress. But some longer words like 'photography' shift the stress. Learning these patterns helps you sound more natural.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say each sentence with the correct intonation. Yes/no questions go UP at the end. Wh-questions and statements go DOWN at the end. Listen to the pattern and copy it.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say these sentences with the correct intonation. Remember: yes/no questions rise, statements and wh-questions fall.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Can you swim? ↗ | I can't swim. ↘ | What do you like doing? ↘ | Do you like reading? ↗ | I like playing football. ↘
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /kən juː swɪm ↗/ | /aɪ kɑːnt swɪm ↘/ | /wɒt duː juː laɪk ˈduː.ɪŋ ↘/ | /duː juː laɪk ˈriː.dɪŋ ↗/ | /aɪ laɪk ˈpleɪ.ɪŋ ˈfʊt.bɔːl ↘/
practicumQuestions.hint: For 'Can you swim?' and 'Do you like reading?', your voice goes UP at the end — these are yes/no questions. For 'What do you like doing?', 'I can't swim', and 'I like playing football', your voice goes DOWN — these are a wh-question and statements.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Intonation carries meaning in English. Rising intonation on yes/no questions signals that you expect a 'yes' or 'no' answer. Falling intonation on statements and wh-questions signals that you are giving information or asking for specific details. Mastering these patterns makes your speech much clearer.
